job.style: a conversation between a teacher and two students

passage: Teacher: Today we are exploring fractions. Remember, a fraction represents a part of a whole, and all parts must be equal in size. If you divide a rectangle into two unequal pieces, you cannot call one piece 1/2. Student A: I thought 1/5 was larger than 1/4 because five is bigger than four. Teacher: Actually, as the denominator increases, the size of each part gets smaller. Imagine sharing a cake; the more people you share with, the smaller your slice becomes. Student B: What about adding fractions like 1/4 and 1/4? Do we add the denominators to get 2/8? Teacher: No, that is a common mistake. When denominators are the same, we only add the numerators, so 1/4 plus 1/4 equals 2/4. Student A: Does multiplying a number by a fraction always make it bigger? Teacher: Not at all. Multiplying by a fraction less than one actually makes the product smaller than the original number. For example, half of ten is five, which is less than ten. Finally, remember that a mixed number like 2 1/3 is a sum, meaning two plus one-third, not two multiplied by one-third. Understanding these rules helps us avoid errors when comparing or calculating with fractions.

items.evidence: If you divide a rectangle into two unequal pieces, you cannot call one piece 1/2.
items.q: Meena cuts a chapati into one big and one small piece. What can she say about the small piece?
options: It is not 1/2, as the pieces are unequal
It is 1/2, as there are two pieces
It is not 1/2, but the bigger piece is
It is 1/2, as both pieces make one whole
items.explain: A fraction needs equal parts, so unequal pieces cannot be called 1/2.

wrong.why: thinks any two pieces are halves, even if unequal
thinks the larger of two pieces is the half
thinks two parts that make a whole must be halves

items.evidence: Actually, as the denominator increases, the size of each part gets smaller.
items.q: Neha gets 1/4 of a pizza and Sam gets 1/5 of the same pizza. Who gets more?
options: Neha, as fourths are bigger than fifths
Sam, as 5 is bigger than 4
Both, as each fraction has 1 on top
Sam, as more parts means more pizza
items.explain: As the denominator grows, each part gets smaller, so 1/4 is more than 1/5.

wrong.why: thinks a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction
thinks bigger numbers in a fraction mean a bigger amount

items.evidence: When denominators are the same, we only add the numerators, so 1/4 plus 1/4 equals 2/4.
items.q: Ravi eats 1/4 of a cake, then another 1/4. How much of the cake has he eaten?
options: 2/4 of the cake
2/8 of the cake
1/8 of the cake
1/16 of the cake
items.explain: The denominators are the same, so add only the numerators: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4.

wrong.why: adds the denominators but keeps one numerator
multiplies the fractions instead of adding them

items.evidence: Multiplying by a fraction less than one actually makes the product smaller than the original number.
items.q: Meera works out 1/2 × 12. What answer should she get?
options: 6, which is smaller than 12
24, which is bigger than 12
12 1/2, which is a bit more than 12
1/24, which is far smaller than 12
items.explain: Multiplying by a fraction less than one gives a smaller product; half of 12 is 6.

wrong.why: thinks multiplying always makes a number bigger
mixes up multiplying by a half with adding a half
multiplies the denominator by 12 instead of taking half

items.evidence: Finally, remember that a mixed number like 2 1/3 is a sum, meaning two plus one-third, not two multiplied by one-third.
items.q: A recipe needs 2 1/3 cups of flour. How much flour is that?
options: Two cups plus a third of a cup
Two cups times a third of a cup
Two cups split into three parts
Two cups plus one cup plus three cups
items.explain: A mixed number is a sum, so 2 1/3 means two plus one-third.

wrong.why: thinks a mixed number means multiplying
thinks the 1/3 divides the two cups
reads the digits as separate whole numbers
